description: We are Computer Science students at UFCG with experience in software development, data analysis, and a shared enthusiasm for astronomy. We are looking for dedicated members to join our project. More than any specific skill, what matters most to us is commitment, dedication, and a genuine willingness to contribute and learn.
summary:
The conditions of the space environment, to which the human body is not naturally adapted, pose a challenge to astronauts' health. Exposure to microgravity causes changes in cardiovascular system functioning, which can become more pronounced during long-duration missions.

In response to this challenge, we developed a system focused on monitoring astronauts' cardiovascular health, using data from medical examinations they already undergo daily. Based on these data, we created an intuitive, organized, and easy-to-understand interface.

The project's main innovation lies in how information is presented. Although health data is already collected and made available to astronauts, it is often displayed through extensive charts containing large amounts of information. Considering the number of health indicators astronauts must monitor during their missions, we aim to make this analysis more straightforward and accessible.

Our solution organizes health indicators into different body systems, using visual elements and a color-coded system to facilitate the identification of potential health changes.

The prototype also has the potential to expand to monitoring other human body systems and can be adapted for applications on Earth, making health monitoring more accessible and easier to understand.

Space is an environment the human body did not evolve for. Microgravity changes how the cardiovascular system works, and these effects can intensify on long-duration missions. Considering this scenario, HemoSpace is a cardiovascular monitoring prototype that turns the measurements astronauts already take every day into a single, easy-to-read screen.

Instead of long charts packed with indicators, HemoSpace organizes the data by body region (head and neck, thorax and heart, upper limbs, lower limbs) on an interactive body map. Each region is colored with a four-color status system: blue for hypoperfusion or volume deficit, green for balance, amber for a moderate alert and red for critical risk. A possible change can be spotted at a glance. Selecting a region opens a short explanation of why it matters, its probable physiological cause, the related space disease hazard cataloged by NASA, recommended countermeasures and a seven-day trend chart. Users can also switch between gravity environments (orbit, Moon, Mars and Earth), and the map adapts its visual fluid-flow cue accordingly.

Data enters the system in three ways: a quick manual form (arm and ankle blood pressure, heart rate, calf variation), an optical PPG reading through the device camera, which estimates heart rate and times capillary refill, and ultrasound images of the jugular and femoral veins. From these inputs, HemoSpace calculates mean arterial pressure, ankle-brachial index and pulse pressure, and classifies each region. In this prototype, ultrasound classification relies on educational samples and the exam type selected by the user. We plan on adding automatic image analysis in future versions.

The main benefit is clarity, as astronauts are not physicians, they should follow many indicators at once. A clear visual summary reduces the amount of data they have to interpret and makes early changes easier to notice. That can help problems be prevented and treated sooner, such as those related to fluid shifts toward the head and Spaceflight Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome (SANS). HemoSpace does not replace medical professionals. Its purpose is to support monitoring and prevention and to work together with qualified health teams. Because the approach is generic, it can be expanded to other body systems and adapted to Earth, for example to help caregivers monitor older adults.

We built the backend in Java (Spring Boot) and the frontend in JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with Chart.js for the charts and the browser’s getUserMedia API for camera access. No dedicated hardware was needed, since the data is already collected daily. The prototype is hosted on GitHub Pages for viewing. HemoSpace is designed to sync online with the team on Earth, but it works fully offline: if the server does not respond within 500 ms, a local engine that mirrors the backend rules computes the result. This matters because communication with Earth is not instantaneous. A future version will add database integration. Given the short deadline, we used LLMs for coding support, brainstorming and image generation, and we included automated tests for the core rules.

The creative contribution lies in how the information is presented. We did not try to collect more data. We made existing exam data understandable through a color-coded body map that works offline and uses the camera as an input.

During our creative process, we researched many factors related to astronaut health, from radiation exposure to mental health. We chose to focus on the circulatory system because problems related to it occur frequently in environments of varying gravity, SANS being one example, and because of technical limitations. We drew on NASA sources about crew health, on the recurrence of circulatory problems and on the constant measurements already taken from crew members. We also reviewed public literature to refine our rules, for example using ankle-brachial index thresholds, a proportional pulse pressure criterion and jugular ultrasound as the main marker for the head region. The thresholds are simplifications for demonstration and are not clinical validation.

Attached are a screenshot of the app’s home screen and the GitHub link with the application running.
